prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.

We represent: habeas petitioner.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that counsel is ineffective under Strickland for failing to investigate and present available mitigating evidence at a capital sentencing.

Cite at least six decisions of the Ninth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. Trial counsel were ineffective at the penalty phase because they failed to investigate and present available mitigating evidence.**

Petitioner must show that counsel's performance was deficient and that the deficiency prejudiced him. *Strickland v. Washington*, 466 U.S. 668, 687–88, 694 (1984). Both showings are met here.

**A. Counsel's failure to investigate was objectively unreasonable.**

Counsel have a duty to make reasonable investigations or to make a reasonable decision that makes particular investigations unnecessary. *Strickland*, 466 U.S. at 691. In a capital case, that duty includes a thorough investigation of the defendant's background. *Wiggins v. Smith*, 539 U.S. 510, 524–25 (2003); *Rompilla v. Beard*, 545 U.S. 374, 387 (2005). The Ninth Circuit has applied these principles repeatedly. It has held that a decision not to present mitigating evidence cannot be called strategic when it rests on an inadequate investigation. *Correll v. Ryan*, 539 F.3d 938, 942–44 (9th Cir. 2008); *Stankewitz v. Woodford*, 365 F.3d 706, 718–20 (9th Cir. 2004).

Counsel here did not meet that standard. They did not obtain readily available school, medical, and institutional records. They did not interview family members who could have described Petitioner's childhood. They did not retain a mental-health expert to evaluate him. Counsel in *Douglas v. Woodford*, 316 F.3d 1079, 1085–90 (9th Cir. 2003), and *Earp v. Ornoski*, 431 F.3d 1158, 1173–77 (9th Cir. 2005), likewise left obvious sources of mitigation unexplored. The court found deficient performance in both cases. The same result follows here.

The timing and scope of the investigation confirm the deficiency. A last-minute, cursory inquiry into mitigation is not a reasonable investigation. *Lambright v. Schriro*, 490 F.3d 1103, 1115–19 (9th Cir. 2007). In *Lambright*, counsel did little to look into the defendant's background and did not follow up on leads that were available to them. *Id.* The same is true of counsel here. The record shows no strategic reason for the omissions. It shows neglect.

Counsel also cannot claim a tactical decision to forgo mitigation. Strategic choices made after less than complete investigation are reasonable only to the extent that reasonable professional judgment supports the limits on the investigation. *Wiggins*, 539 U.S. at 521–23. The Ninth Circuit has refused to defer to "strategy" that was in fact the product of inattention. *Jennings v. Woodford*, 290 F.3d 1006, 1014–19 (9th Cir. 2002); *Bean v. Calderon*, 163 F.3d 1073, 1077–80 (9th Cir. 1998). Counsel could not have made an informed choice to omit this evidence, because they never learned what it was.

**B. The omitted evidence creates a reasonable probability of a different sentence.**

Prejudice requires a "reasonable probability that, but for counsel's unprofessional errors, the result of the proceeding would have been different." *Strickland*, 466 U.S. at 694. A reasonable probability is one sufficient to undermine confidence in the outcome. *Id.* The question is whether there is a reasonable probability that at least one juror would have voted against death if the jury had heard the full mitigation case. *See Wiggins*, 539 U.S. at 537; *Porter v. McCollum*, 558 U.S. 30, 41–42 (2009) (per curiam). Courts must reweigh the aggravating evidence against the totality of the mitigating evidence, both what was presented at trial and what was available. *Williams v. Taylor*, 529 U.S. 362, 397–98 (2000).

The jury heard almost nothing about Petitioner's life. The evidence counsel left undiscovered would have shown severe childhood deprivation, abuse, and impaired mental functioning. The Ninth Circuit has found prejudice on comparable omissions. *Correll*, 539 F.3d at 951–52; *Stankewitz*, 365 F.3d at 722–25; *Douglas*, 316 F.3d at 1090–92; *Earp*, 431 F.3d at 1177–79; *Lambright*, 490 F.3d at 1124–29. Evidence of this kind bears directly on Petitioner's moral culpability. It also rebuts the prosecution's portrayal of him as an incorrigible offender. The prosecution's case in aggravation was not overwhelming, and the sentencing verdict turned on a jury that knew nothing of Petitioner's history. There is a reasonable probability that at least one juror, hearing that history, would have voted for life.

Because counsel's deficient performance prejudiced Petitioner, this Court should grant the writ as to the death sentence.
